title: Cops detail intense struggle to inquest
article: Const. Kyle Petre described Larry McPherson as "the hardest person I've ever had to restrain" on the second day of the coroner's inquest into McPherson's death.

Petre, who testified Thursday, was one of five officers who wrestled to bring McPherson under control after he was seen smashing a squeegee into the window of a Shell gas station and throwing rocks through other windows just before 1 a.m. on Aug. 28, 2007.
Petre described how he and four other officers first held McPherson down as he thrashed and kicked and swung his head around on the pavement of 100th Street.
Petre said he used his knee to hold one leg down while holding the other with both hands, twisting it to induce pain, in an unsuccessful bid to stop him from kicking.
When Const. Matt Shearer forced the handcuffs on McPherson, the four officers attempted to pick him up and carry him into the back of a police cruiser.
However, Petre said McPherson kept kicking and could have damaged the car, so they laid him down to restrain his ankles.
When they picked him up again to put him in the car, McPherson went limp.
"He went from extremely violent thrashing to as if he were sleeping," Petre said. "It was just like a switch went off."
After checking his pulse, Petre said McPherson went into a seizure, his muscles seized up and he shook violently on the ground with foamy drool seeping out of his mouth.
Const. Gerry Sliworsky, who also testified Thursday, said he immediately called for an ambulance while the other officers gave McPherson a blanket and put a towel under his head.
By the time the ambulance arrived at 1:11 a.m., paramedic Sally Wiltse said McPherson had regained consciousness and was thrashing violently, trying to push the four officers off him.
She waited for two minutes for him to stop so she could examine him, but he kept fighting.
"He was lifting all four of them off the ground," she said.
After Wiltse had pulled out her equipment and McPherson had fought for four minutes straight, she said he went limp.
She found he wasn't breathing and had no pulse, and immediately administered CPR, but he didn't wake up. McPherson was pronounced dead at hospital shortly after 1:30 a.m.
Wiltse said what she saw met the description of cocaine psychosis.
"It takes them over and makes them become something else," she said, adding no person under normal circumstances could keep fighting like he did.
However, she also said she wasn't informed that McPherson had been unconscious or experienced a seizure when she received the call - information that she said could have helped her prepare.
McPherson was put on the trajectory toward his death several days earlier, according to the friend he was staying with at the Caravan Motel.

Todd Gobout, who testified via video-conferencing from Terrace, said he and McPherson had ordered an eightball of cocaine, or 2.7 grams of rock, from a man at the former Wet Spot Bar on the morning of Aug 24.
But they didn't recognize the man who knocked on their hotel room door a few hours later to deliver the drugs.
"He just said 'it's party time' and walked in," said Gobout, adding McPherson threw the man of the hotel.
A minute later, the man they spoke to at the Wet Spot came in, explained what happened and made the sale, but Gobout said the man they threw out returned hours later looking for a fight.
McPherson, who had already smoked all of the drugs, swung the hotel T.V. around as a weapon, scaring them off and smashing the hotel window.
After that incident they moved to the Cedar Lodge. And on the night of Aug. 26 they decided to get high again.

In the span of six hours, McPherson had smoked nearly five grams of crack cocaine and drank about six ounces of vodka, Gobout said, when a man banged on their window and shined car lights into the room just before midnight.
McPherson panicked and bolted out the room, and Gobout said he never saw him again.
The inquiry is expected to wrap up today with the testimony from the doctors who conducted the autopsy, toxicology and other medical reports, as well as McPherson's sister Lori McPherson.
Afterward, the jury will come to a decision on the cause of death as well as recommendations on how to improve practices to prevent similar deaths in the future.
